oneLineAnswer: A prescription anti-seizure medicine for epilepsy that has not responded to other drugs, and for infantile spasms in babies.
whatItIs:
Vigabatrin is a prescription anti-seizure medicine, also called an antiepileptic drug. You take it by mouth, as a tablet or as a powder stirred into water. Brand names include Sabril, Vigadrone and Vigafyde. It is also called gamma-vinyl GABA.

Nerves pass messages using chemicals called neurotransmitters. GABA is the main calming neurotransmitter in the brain. Vigabatrin is shaped like GABA. It attaches to and permanently disables GABA transaminase, or GABA-T, the enzyme that normally clears GABA away. With GABA-T disabled, GABA builds up in the central nervous system.

Chemically, vigabatrin is 4-amino-5-hexenoic acid. Its formula is C6H11NO2, and its molecular weight is about 129. It was first sold as an epilepsy drug in the United Kingdom in 1989. The United States approved it in 2009, under tight restrictions because of an eye risk.
whatItDoes: It raises the level of GABA, a signal that damps down overactive nerve firing.
Blocking GABA-T is thought to explain its anti-seizure effect.
The exact way it stops seizures is not known.
It is used as an add-on for hard-to-treat partial seizures in people aged 2 and older.
It is used alone for infantile spasms, a seizure disorder that begins in babies.
howPeopleUseIt: In the United States it is approved for only two situations.
The first is refractory complex partial seizures in people aged 2 and older. The label means seizures that did not improve after several other treatments.
For that use it is added to other treatment, and it is not a first-choice drug.
The second is infantile spasms, a seizure disorder that starts in babies. It is used alone in babies aged 1 month to 2 years.
For infantile spasms, a doctor must judge that the likely benefit outweighs the risk of vision loss.
It is sold as a 500 mg tablet and as a powder for oral solution.
In the United States it comes only through the Vigabatrin REMS Program. Prescribers and pharmacies must enroll, and each patient is enrolled too.
Eyes are checked before or soon after starting, then at least every 3 months, and once more after stopping.
Doctors are told to stop it if it is not clearly helping.
That review comes at about 3 months for partial seizures, and at 2 to 4 weeks for infantile spasms.
Researchers have also tested it in other conditions.
Those include status epilepticus after oxygen loss, cocaine dependence and autoimmune encephalitis.
Those studies do not show that it works for those uses.

commonSideEffects: Headache, sleepiness and tiredness are common.
Dizziness, shaky hands called tremor, and clumsy coordination are common.
Blurred vision and double vision are common.
Nausea, diarrhea and weight gain are common.
Memory trouble, insomnia and irritability are common.
Colds, sore throat and other upper respiratory infections are common.
Depression and a rash are reported.
In babies treated for infantile spasms, the common problems were sleepiness, bronchitis, ear infection and acute otitis media.
Anemia, meaning too few red blood cells, is also listed.
So are peripheral neuropathy, meaning nerve damage in the hands and feet, and edema, meaning swelling.
seriousSigns: The main serious risk is permanent loss of side vision. Side vision is what you see out of the corner of your eye.
Both eyes narrow their field of view. Severe cases leave only a small central tunnel, which can disable a person.
Sometimes the central retina is damaged too, so sharpness of sight falls.
Adult studies suggest 30 percent or more of patients develop this narrowing.
The timing is unpredictable. It can begin within weeks, or only after months or years.
Higher doses and longer exposure raise the risk. No dose or exposure is known to be free of risk.
People often do not notice the loss until it is severe.
The loss does not reverse when the drug is stopped.
Some infants develop abnormal MRI signal changes in the brain. Whether those changes cause harm is unresolved.
Like other anti-seizure drugs, it can raise the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior.
It can cause sleepiness and fatigue that make driving or using machines unsafe.
Stopping it suddenly can cause withdrawal seizures, so it is reduced gradually.
Rarely, serious liver injury has been reported. A firm link has not been proven.
whoShouldAvoid: The label lists no contraindications, meaning no group is barred outright.
People who already have other permanent vision loss should not use it.
That also covers people at high risk of such loss.
The exception is when the benefit clearly outweighs the risk.
It should not be combined with other drugs that can badly damage the eye.
Examples are drugs that cause retinopathy or glaucoma.
Again, unless the benefit clearly outweighs the risk.
It is not a first-choice drug for complex partial seizures. It is for people who have already failed several treatments.
It is not established for complex partial seizures in children under 2.
It is also not established for infantile spasms in babies under 1 month.
Pregnant women need a careful risk discussion. See the pregnancy section.
Do not drive or use machinery until you know how it affects you.

interactions: Phenytoin: vigabatrin may moderately lower total phenytoin blood levels, so the phenytoin dose may need adjusting.
Clonazepam: vigabatrin may moderately raise peak clonazepam levels, which can increase clonazepam side effects.
Rufinamide: its blood levels may drop slightly to moderately. Whether that matters clinically is not settled.
Phenobarbital and sodium valproate: no clinically significant interaction with vigabatrin was found.
Carbamazepine, clorazepate, primidone and sodium valproate appear not to change vigabatrin blood levels.
Steroid oral contraceptives: vigabatrin is unlikely to reduce their effectiveness.
Liver blood tests: vigabatrin lowers the enzymes ALT and AST in up to 90 percent of patients.
This can hide early liver injury from a routine liver test.
Urine tests: vigabatrin can raise urine amino acids and cause a false positive for some rare inherited metabolic disorders.
Vigabatrin induces the liver enzyme CYP2C9, which can affect how some other drugs are handled.
pregnancyAndChildren: There are no adequate human data on the risk of vigabatrin in pregnancy. Case reports and cohort studies have not shown a clear rise in birth defects or miscarriage. However, animal studies at clinically relevant doses found fetal harm. Rabbits had more malformations, mainly cleft palate, and more fetal deaths. Rats had lower fetal weights and more anatomical variations. A pregnancy registry tracks outcomes for women who take anti-seizure drugs. For children, effectiveness is established for add-on treatment of refractory complex partial seizures from age 2 to 16. It is also established for infantile spasms from 1 month to 2 years. It is not established below those ages. Eye testing is hard in babies, so vision damage may be found late. One analysis of a Canadian study suggested that 6 months of treatment is enough for infantile spasms. Prescribers still judge each case. Limited data suggest that maternal doses up to 2000 mg daily put only small amounts into breast milk. That is far less than the dose given to infants. No effects in a breastfed baby would be expected.
whatWeDoNotKnow: The exact way vigabatrin stops seizures is not known.
No dose and no length of treatment has been shown to be free of the vision risk.
How often and how severely babies and children lose vision is poorly measured, because testing their eyes is hard.
Whether the abnormal MRI scans seen in some infants mean real harm is unresolved.
There are no adequate human data on vigabatrin use in pregnancy.
The FDA review said it had no definitive evidence that the required eye monitoring prevents vision damage.
The FDA review also said the three main infantile spasms efficacy studies did not meet the agency's usual standards.
Whether rare cases of serious liver injury are truly caused by vigabatrin has not been convincingly established.

NCCIH has no vigabatrin page; the URL returned HTTP 404, so no NCCIH citation appears here.
The NINDS infantile spasms page redirected to a general NINDS epilepsy page that does not mention vigabatrin, so it could not support any claim.
A guessed FDA press release URL for the 2009 Sabril approval returned HTTP 404. FDA approval documents under accessdata.fda.gov were used instead.
MedlinePlus drug monographs were excluded as copyrighted third-party content. No MedlinePlus health topic or medical test summary specific to vigabatrin was found.
NCBI Bookshelf search results were also blocked by the same reCAPTCHA check, so no Bookshelf page other than through PubChem was used.
No dosage or personal protocol information is given anywhere in this record, by design.
Exact rates for individual side effects differ between the adult add-on studies and the infantile spasms studies; per-reaction percentages are not reported here.
The brand-name Sabril label was retrieved for cross-checking but every claim cited comes from the generic-name vigabatrin label record or the sources listed.
No source fetched here states how common vigabatrin use is, or how often vision loss leads to disability in practice.
summary: This record covers what vigabatrin is, the two seizure conditions it is approved for, its permanent vision-loss risk, its interactions, and the questions that remain open.
